The truth is, I’ve loved making games since I was a student. But game jobs in Vietnam were very limited, and the salaries weren’t high. Making a game solo was also extremely difficult before AI. And right now, my app revenue already gives me a pretty comfortable life, so I’m making games for fun lol.

content:
After I posted 2 videos about the game I built entirely with AI, a lot of people didn’t believe it was real.

Well, here’s the video showing how I built the full Star Defender game using Claude Fable 5 + Rork.

In total, it took me around 5 hours: about 1 hour to build the gameplay, and another 4 hours to turn it into an almost complete game. It also cost around 1,500 Rork credits, which is about $300 based on Rork’s pricing.

Also, Rork already has built-in integrations for generating game art, sound effects, code..., so I didn’t use any external tools at all.

As I mentioned in my previous video, I wanted to test Claude Fable 5 to make a game, and since I’m a Rork partner, I had free credits to use.

I also only used natural language prompts, mixing both Vietnamese and English. There were no complex prompts or prompt engineering involved.

Yes, I only prompted. I didn’t touch any code. I was basically just acting as a game tester: playing the game, taking screenshots whenever I found bugs, and describing them so the AI could fix them.

And honestly, it performed better than I expected.

At first, I only wanted to test how well Fable 5 could build games. But now, I want to experiment with building a game from scratch all the way to releasing it on the App Store, including AdMob integration and in-game purchases to monetize it.

You don’t always need to over-optimize conversion.

Sometimes the easiest lever is just increasing your subscription price.

And that can increase perceived value too.

Don’t underprice yourself too early.

content:
If you want to grow an app to $10k/month, distribution matters more than the product.

From my experience, the 4 best beginner-friendly marketing channels are:

1. Organic TikTok slideshows
- Easy to make. Can get millions of views.
- But not always the best for paid conversion.

2. Organic AI influencers/UGC
- Better conversion, but expensive and hard to scale.
- You need a real workflow before building an AI UGC army.

3. Hiring paid influencers/UGC
- Can work really well.
- But creator quality is inconsistent, outreach takes forever, and good influencers are not cheap.

4. Paid ads (Meta Ads, Tiktok Ads, Google Ads, Apple Search Ads)
- The fastest way to scale MRR.
- But margins drop fast if your niche or funnel doesn’t convert well.

No channel is perfect.
The real unlock is stacking channels:

organic + influencers + AI UGC + paid ads.
That’s how you scale. 😌

content:
This is the full video showing what I made with Rork and Claude Fable 5.

It’s super simple because I wanted to test Fable 5 using completely natural language (and even in Vietnamese) to see how well it would perform without any fancy prompts and it worked surprisingly well.

I simply uploaded screenshots of Subway Surfers and told it to "clone this," and it did a pretty solid job.

Also, Rork already has built-in integrations to generate game art, sound effects, and 3D models, so I didn’t use any external tools at all. It cost me around 500–600 credits.

As I mentioned in my previous video, I wanted to test Claude Fable 5, and since I’m a Rork partner, I had free credits to use.

Right now, instead of using Claude Code and then wiring up separate 3D tools and everything else which takes way too much time and $, I just use Rork to build everything and showcase it here. So yeah, that’s my workflow.

content:
Most of my coding doesn't need a frontier model on every turn.

Burning Opus or GPT-5.5 tokens on routine edits, refactors, test fixes, small UI changes... adds up fast.

And honestly, most of that work doesn't need the top model.

Open-weight models have caught up enough that GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.7-Code, and DeepSeek V4 Pro can already handle a real share of day-to-day coding tasks.

But the model is only half the story.

The harness matters just as much:
how the agent reads your repo,
runs tools,
understands terminal output,
fixes failed edits,
and keeps moving without breaking everything.

That’s why I’m testing ClinePass.

It puts a curated set of open-weight models behind one $9.99/mo sub inside Cline, while still letting you bring your own key or run local when a task actually needs it.

Pointing it at my own repos this week to see where the line really is. 💪

content:
Warm up matters more than people think.

I usually warm up a new TikTok account for 2–3 days before posting.

If it gets low views or 0 views, I stop posting for a few days, warm it up again, then post.

But if your video gets 300–500 views and stops, that’s usually not shadowban.

TikTok already tested your video with a small audience.

They just didn’t care.

That means the account is fine.

The content is cooked. 

And congrats to this guy.

content:
I can confirm this is true. A lot of people think getting under 1,000 views means they’re shadowbanned, but that’s usually not the case. It’s simply because your content isn’t good enough yet.

As shown in the image below, even if you’re a real person posting from a real device with a real IP, if your content doesn’t match the current trend, your views can still stay low like normal.

I’ve had many accounts get 0 views or under 500 views, but once I stopped posting and changed the content, the views came back strong.

That’s why, with TikTok, we need volume to increase the chances of going viral.

Meanwhile, on the 3 phones below, I only started posting less than 2 months ago. There are 6 accounts in total, and none of them are shadow banned. The average is around 10K views per post, with quite a few posts getting over 100K views. All phones are using VPNs.

This has helped me get an average of 700 new users per app every day.

So I think if your views are flopping, it’s likely because you set up something wrong, your content has visuals that violate TikTok’s policies, your IP is blacklisted, or simply your content isn’t good enough for TikTok to keep pushing it viral.

content:
Don’t just build the app you need.

Build the app users actually want.

But if you only build for money, you’ll probably get bored during marketing, product, and iteration.

The best place to build is somewhere in the middle:

content:
One of my TikTok posts from 3 days ago has started picking up nicely, reaching 61K views with 84% (and still growing) of the audience coming from the US, using a VPN-only setup.

As I mentioned before, TikTok doesn’t ban VPNs. What gets flagged are low-quality or heavily abused VPN IPs that have been used for spam. The most important factor is still the content. If your content doesn’t resonate with the audience in the country you’re targeting, you’ll likely get stuck at 100–2,000 views, regardless of whether you’re using a VPN or not.

And if you’re already in the US, you don’t need a VPN at all, just using a local SIM card is enough.

content:
Normal day of building in public.

One thing I’ve learned:

I only publicly share apps in saturated markets.

For apps in unique niches, I even publish them under separate developer accounts.

Why?

Because if your growth comes from organic traffic, every screenshot, revenue chart, and strategy thread is free market research for competitors.

If your app runs 100% on paid ads, share everything. Competitors can copy your product, but they still need to buy users.

But if you’ve found a niche with strong organic virality, silence is often the best moat.

Build quietly.
Scale quietly.
Dominate quietly.

Then, when the market is saturated and you’re already the #1 player, tell the story.

Building in public is great.

Until you realize you’re accidentally onboarding your future competitors. 🥴

content:
I like this way of thinking:

Don’t build something just because you’re passionate about it while users don’t actually need it.

And don’t blindly build random apps either.

Find the distribution angle first.

My workflow:

>  Find viral content in a specific niche
> Study the hooks, formats, pain points, and comments
> Identify what users are already interested in
> Check whether the niche can monetize through subscriptions or one-time purchases
> Test different content angles before building
> Build the simplest app that solves the problem
> Create content using the formats that already proved they can go viral
> Track views, installs, conversion, retention, and revenue
> Improve the product based on real user behavior
> Scale the best-performing channels with more organic content or paid ads

Distribution first. Product second.

The key is to behave as human as possible.

content:
Every vibe coder needs to understand this 👇

Not advanced engineering.

Just the boring basics that save you from breaking everything.

Non-negotiables:

> .env = secrets live here
> Never push .env to GitHub
>npm run dev = local only
> package.json = scripts, dependencies, versions
> npm run build = what actually ships
> npm packages = install / remove / update carefully
> git add .env = instant regret
> localhost:3000 ≠ a real URL
> env vars ≠ hardcoded values
> terminal errors are not decoration

Nice-to-know stuff that saves days:

> npm i --legacy-peer-deps when packages fight
> .gitignore = files Git should ignore
> basic Git: clone, pull, commit, push
> DB schemas / SQL if your app stores data
> auth basics: users, sessions, tokens
> dev words: components, modals, cards, routes
> reading docs > randomly guessing
> asking AI clear questions > “fix this bro”

You don’t need to be a “real dev.”

You just need to understand enough to ship without nuking your own app.

Happy vibe coding ✌️

content:
I once quit my job and used my savings to build an app, and then failed badly.

A lot of people ask me about quitting their job to build something, and I always try to stop them.

Because once you quit your job, the financial pressure and stress can crush your motivation to keep building.

In the early days, most apps usually make no revenue, or very little revenue.

Don’t believe those brainless tweets on X like:

“My app made $10k in 2 weeks.”

Lol. That is either an extremely rare lucky case, or they spent a lot of money on paid ads and influencers.

And trust me, if you don’t have experience with ads, you will most likely lose money in the beginning.

Quit your job only when your app is already generating enough profit (profit, not revenue) to cover your normal living expenses. 😃

content:
Must-read if you want to promote an app or sell any product on TikTok or IG.

And here are a few updates based on my experience. The 4 best methods I’ve seen for beginners are:

1. TikTok slideshows
Easy to make and capable of getting high views, but harder to convert into paying users.

2. AI influencers
Usually convert better, but they’re quite expensive and take a lot of time to build a proper workflow and scale an AI UGC army.

3. Hiring influencers
Works pretty well, but the downside is that it costs a lot of money. Sometimes influencers put in minimal effort, so you need strong quality control. It’s also very time-consuming to DM people individually, search for, and filter high-quality influencers.

4. Paid ads
The biggest advantage is that you can scale MRR very quickly. But the downside is lower profit margins, and you need to choose the right app niche with high conversion rates to stay profitable while running ads.

Each method has tradeoffs. The best strategy is usually combining multiple distribution channels together. 😌

People underestimate how far AI UGC has already gone.

content:
From my experience observing and testing both paid ads and organic:

If your app is painful + hard paywall (like looksmaxing, height increase, weight loss…), you can become profitable from day one.

But for “vitamin” apps with trials (like note takers, AI wrappers, habit trackers…), you’ll almost always take losses upfront and only make profit through yearly renewals which means you must keep churn low.

Organic, on the other hand, works for almost everything but it requires a lot of upfront effort.

The top profitable apps all use both.

content:
You can share your SaaS on X that’s totally fine, you’ll get customers.

But if you share your B2C mobile app on X, you’ll almost get no users just more competitors and 1-star reviews from them. They don’t hate your product maybe they don’t even use your product., they just leave 1-star reviews because they like doing it.

That’s why I barely share my B2C products anymore. The ones I’ve made public are already saturated markets. For niche products, I won’t share them maybe I’ll share when the market is saturated lol. Just kidding… but seriously, be careful when sharing your B2C apps.

Your B2C users are not on X.

Spend your time on TikTok and Instagram much better.

X is for SaaS.

content:
If you want your organic content to convert, you need a strong and natural CTA that makes users feel compelled to download your app.

The formula is actually simple:

Start with a painful problem your users face → provide useful knowledge to help them solve it → show how your app supports that solution → then add a CTA as if an AI influencer genuinely used your app and successfully solved the problem.

content:
How to create multiple AI Influencer variants (step-by-step) using Claude Opus 4.7 + Arcads Workflow.

This is how you scale content WITHOUT hiring creators 👇

Step 1: Find a viral reference

Go to TikTok
→ search your niche (fitness, study, looksmaxing, etc.)
→ find 1 influencer video with high views

You don’t need originality
You need what already works
Step 2: Turn image → JSON → variants
Take screenshots from that video
Drop into Claude Opus 4.7

Prompt it like:
“Convert this person into a structured JSON prompt for image generation + create 5–10 variants (different face, hair, pose, vibe)”

Now you have:

1 base character
5–10 variations
→ same identity, different “angles”

This is your UGC army

Step 3: Scale images with Arcads

Inside Arcads:

Create a workflow
Paste each JSON variant from Claude
Add a nanobanana image block (or any image gen model)

Duplicate block = number of variants

Now you’re generating:

→ multiple influencers
→ in parallel
→ fully automated

Step 4: Turn images → video
Create ONE master prompt:
“Generate a short-form video of this character posing / walking / talking with subtle motion, cinematic lighting, viral TikTok style”
Then:

Connect all image outputs
→ into 1 AI video generation block

Now you get:
→ multiple videos
→ same format
→ different characters
Why this works

You’re not creating content

You’re building a system that prints content

Variants = more hooks

More hooks = more chances to go viral

More viral = more installs / revenue
Real insight most people miss:

1 influencer = 1 chance
10 variants = 10 chances

Distribution beats perfection.

content:
A lot of people ask me if I get shadowbanned. The answer is yes this is one of my accounts that got shadowbanned. From my experience, around 20–30% of accounts get shadowbanned.

How do you handle these accounts?

Usually, if the account isn’t fully banned, it can recover. You just need to stop posting for a while and leave it there. I’ve had a few accounts like this. I just let them sit and use them like a normal user (scroll, like, share) for about 5–10 minutes a day. After 1–2 months, when I start posting again, getting 1K–100K views is pretty normal.

But if you’re getting 0 views on multiple videos in a row, just abandon that account.

I agree with this point. Another reason I don’t run ads for my mobile app is that I already have to give up 15%/30% to the App Store, plus around 7% in taxes. If I set up a company, the total tax could go up to about 25%. That means even before ads and maintenance costs, I’m already losing around 22–55% of my revenue.

If I add ads and the margins aren’t high, as an indie hacker with no VC or investors like me, I’d probably go bankrupt. So for now, I’m focusing on organic growth, and I’ll save paid ads for my web products.

For me, I’d still take a $10k/month project with $9k profit over a $50k/month one with only $5k profit lol. 😌

content:
I really like people who show the truth like Adam.

The reason I don’t run ads something people often ask is because my app is for students and follows a freemium model, so there’s a high chance of losing money if I run ads.

I actually tested Meta Ads with around $1k, and my cost per install was about $7 (probably because my skills aren’t great lol). The revenue I got back was only around $50 bruh, I’d go bankrupt if I kept testing and failing like that.

And even if you are profitable, you still have to subtract another 15%–30% fee from Apple. You need to burn a lot of cash for the algorithm to learn before you can become profitable. Plus, your app has to convert extremely well like those looksmaxing or height-growth apps with hard paywall.

Ads are actually great if you’re VC-backed or have a big budget.

And remember, don’t share your viral format. If it gets copied everywhere, it’ll saturate quickly and people will get bored.

content:
I found 2 more AI influencer accounts that are in growth mode right now.

What’s interesting:
in the early stage, they don’t promote anything.

They just post consistently to grow the account first:

- followers
- reach
- engagement
- trust

Only after the account has enough momentum do they start promoting products.

That’s actually a very smart IG strategy.

I think this might also be one reason I failed on Instagram:
I promoted my product too early, before the account had enough followers and enough trust.

Instagram feels very different from TikTok here.

On TikTok, you can sometimes push product earlier if the content hits.
On IG, it feels like you need to build the audience first, then monetize.

Good reminder for me:
grow the page first, sell later.

content:
“This idea already exists.”

Good. That’s not a problem, that’s validation.

What it actually tells you:
– The market is real.
– People are already paying for this.
– Demand is proven, not hypothetical.

You don’t need to convince anyone this should exist.
You just need to do it better.

You’re not here to invent something from scratch.
You’re here to improve what already works 
make it simpler, faster, cheaper, and distribute it better.

Look at history:
– Google wasn’t the first search engine.
– Facebook wasn’t the first social network.
– TikTok wasn’t the first video app.

They didn’t win by being first.
They won by being better and by getting in front of more people.

At the end of the day:
Execution beats originality.

content:
Lesson 3: A lot of people think that when they use a VPN and get stuck at 100–200 or 800–1000 views, it means they’re shadow-banned.

That’s not entirely true.

Try posting on your own account in your own country you can still get stuck at 100–200 or 800–1000 views. That’s completely normal, this is content issues.

TikTok is just much harder now than before.

If you’re using a free VPN or a shared IP with too many users, you’ll likely get banned right when creating the account not shadow-banned later.

content:
The simplest way to create an AI influencer using workflow (3 steps):

Nano Banana → Veo 3 → Arcads AI Workflow

Step 1: Build your character with a JSON prompt (Nano Banana Workflow)
→ Use a structured JSON prompt instead of writing random text
→ Define the look clearly: character, outfit, lighting, camera style, background
→ Add negative constraints like: no logos, no text, no extra fingers, no CGI skin, no warped mirror

This makes the output more stable and reusable.
You’re not just prompting.
You’re building a repeatable image system

Step 2: Turn image → video (Veo 3 Workflow)
→ Connect the Nano Banana output directly into Veo 3
→ Add a simple motion prompt: slight body movement, natural head turn, subtle phone movement
→ Keep it minimal so it feels more real
Workflow removes the manual back-and-forth.

Step 3: Add script + voice (Arcads AI Workflow)
→ Feed the generated video into Arcads AI
→ Add a short script, usually 10–20 seconds
→ Generate voice + lipsync that matches the character vibe

Now the character becomes actual content.
Why workflow matters:
Prompt → Image → Video → Voice

No messy manual process.
No repeating the same setup every time.
Just a clean pipeline you can scale.

Nano Banana + Veo 3 + Arcads AI + workflow feature
= simple AI influencer factory
